claim: Most cellular features have a range of states.
source: Most cellular features have a range of states, but understanding the mechanisms responsible for interspecific divergence is a challenge for evolutionary cell biology.
evidence: This is a general statement about cellular features presented in the abstract without specific supporting data in the manuscript.

claim: Mean phenotypes will deviate from optimal states to a degree depending on the effective population size.
source: Mean phenotypes will deviate from optimal states to a degree depending on the effective population size, potentially leading to substantial divergence in the absence of diversifying selection.
evidence: This claim is supported by the mathematical models developed in the manuscript, particularly Equations (13b) and (14a).

claim: The steady-state distribution for the mean can be bimodal, with one domain being largely driven by selection and the other by mutation pressure.
source: The steady-state distribution for the mean can even be bimodal, with one domain being largely driven by selection and the other by mutation pressure, leading to the illusion of phenotypic shifts being induced by movement among alternative adaptive domains.
evidence: This is demonstrated theoretically in the manuscript and illustrated in Figure 4.

claim: Most cellular features vary among individuals within populations in a nearly continuous fashion.
source: As with nearly all biological traits, most cellular features vary among individuals within populations in a nearly continuous fashion, owing to genetic differences among individuals and the myriad of stochastic factors experienced by all organisms (ranging from intrinsic cellular noise to external environmental forces; Lynch and Walsh, 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Lynch and Walsh, 1998.

claim: Catalytic rates, rates of gene expression and intracellular transport, and numbers and sizes of organelles vary continuously within species.
source: This is true, for example, for catalytic rates, rates of gene expression and intracellular transport, numbers and sizes of organelles, etc.
evidence: This is presented as examples of continuous variation in cellular features.

claim: Some fraction of within-species genetic variation is transformed into among-species divergence as alternative alleles arise by mutation and proceed to fixation.
source: Ultimately, some fraction of within-species genetic variation is transformed into among-species divergence as alternative alleles arise by mutation and in some cases proceed to fixation (Wright, 1969; Walsh and Lynch, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Wright, 1969 and Walsh and Lynch, 2018.

claim: The magnitude of phenotypic divergence is dictated by three major evolutionary factors: the pattern of selection, the rate of origin and distribution of mutational effects, and the power of random genetic drift.
source: The magnitude of such divergence is dictated by three major evolutionary factors: the pattern of selection (the phenotypic fitness function), which imposes a directional and/or stabilizing force on the mean phenotype; the rate of origin and distribution of mutational effects, which define the raw materials upon which natural selection operates; and the power of random genetic drift, which imposes noise on the selective process.
evidence: This is a theoretical framework statement based on established evolutionary theory.

claim: The internal environment of cells remains largely constant over long time scales and broad geographic locations due to homeostatic effects.
source: In contrast, owing to homeostatic effects, the internal environment of cells remains largely constant over long time scales and broad geographic locations, raising the possibility of establishing general evolutionary principles that transcend the imposition of transient ecological changes.
evidence: This is presented as a general biological principle about cellular homeostasis.

claim: The stationary distribution of mean phenotypes is proportional to the product of the distributions expected under selection alone and under mutation alone.
source: showing that the stationary distribution of mean phenotypes (conditional on a particular level of genetic variance, a point that will be returned to below) is proportional to the product of the distributions expected under selection alone and under mutation alone.
evidence: This is derived mathematically from Equation (1b) in the manuscript.

claim: Most quantitative traits have an approximately normal phenotype distribution on some scale of measurement.
source: We will make use of the fact that most quantitative traits have an approximately normal phenotype distribution on some scale of measurement, which follows from the central limit theorem (Lynch and Walsh, 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by the central limit theorem and citation to Lynch and Walsh, 1998.

claim: The change in mean phenotype caused by selection is equal to the product of the genetic variance for the trait and the gradient in the logarithm of mean fitness with respect to mean phenotype.
source: This expression states that, provided the phenotype distribution is normal, the change in mean phenotype caused by selection is equal to the product of the genetic variance for the trait and the gradient in the logarithm of mean fitness with respect to mean phenotype.
evidence: This is derived mathematically from Equation (7) in the manuscript.

claim: Evolution by natural selection comes to a standstill when there is no genetic variance for the trait or the phenotypic mean resides at a point where the slope of the function of mean fitness with respect to mean phenotype is zero.
source: Evolution by natural selection comes to a standstill when there is no genetic variance for the trait or the phenotypic mean resides at a point where the slope of the function of mean fitness with respect to mean phenotype is zero.
evidence: This is a logical inference from Equation (7) in the manuscript.

claim: Protein-protein interactions typically depend on no more than a few dozen amino-acid sites.
source: Protein-protein interactions (e.g. the interfaces between dimeric molecules) typically depend on no more than a few dozen amino-acid sites.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge about protein structure.

claim: The catalytic sites of enzymes often consist of a small-to-moderate numbers of residues that either facilitate or inhibit catalytic rates.
source: Likewise, the catalytic sites of enzymes often consist of a small-to-moderate numbers of residues that either facilitate or inhibit catalytic rates, and the sizes of intracellular organelles and cytoskeletal components are constrained by cell size.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge about enzyme structure.

claim: Phenotypic variance reduces the efficiency of selection by diminishing the correspondence between genotype and phenotype.
source: As will be seen repeatedly below, phenotypic variance (an inevitable consequence of external environmental and internal cellular effects) generally reduces the efficiency of selection by diminishing the correspondence between genotype and phenotype.
evidence: This is a theoretical inference from the mathematical models presented.

claim: The inverse scaling of mutation rate with Ne is qualitatively consistent with the drift-barrier hypothesis for mutation-rate evolution.
source: Such a scaling is qualitatively consistent with the drift-barrier hypothesis for mutation-rate evolution (Lynch, 2010; Lynch, 2011), which postulates that because most mutations are deleterious, selection will typically operate to improve replication fidelity, with refinements in molecular performance eventually being thwarted by random genetic drift – as the mutation rate is progressively lowered, there is less room for improvement and hence a narrower range of selectively advantageous replication-fidelity variants accessible by selection.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Lynch, 2010 and Lynch, 2011.

claim: Bacteria utilize transcription-factor binding-site motifs with stronger affinity to their cognate transcription factors than is the case in eukaryotes.
source: The fact that bacteria utilize transcription-factor binding-site motifs with stronger affinity to their cognate transcription factors than is the case in eukaryotes is also plausibly related to a higher efficiency of selection in the former (Lynch and Hagner, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Lynch and Hagner, 2015.

claim: Proteins typically evolve to the 'margin of stability,' such that only one or two mutations are usually enough to destabilize the folding process.
source: Finally, proteins typically evolve to the 'margin of stability,' such that only one or two mutations are usually enough to destabilize the folding process (Taverna and Goldstein, 2002; Tokuriki and Tawfik, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Taverna and Goldstein, 2002 and Tokuriki and Tawfik, 2009.

claim: Protein stability is positively associated with fitness because destabilized proteins are prone to loss of function, aggregation, and/or direct toxicity.
source: Protein stability is deemed to be positively associated with fitness because destabilized proteins are prone to loss of function, aggregation, and/or direct toxicity.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge about protein stability and fitness.

claim: It is relatively easy to obtain more stable proteins by mutagenesis.
source: Strikingly, however, it is relatively easy to obtain more stable proteins by mutagenesis (Matsuura et al., 1999; Bershtein et al., 2013; Sullivan et al., 2012), with the contributing residues typically interacting in an additive fashion (Wells, 1990; Serrano et al., 1993; Zhang et al., 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Matsuura et al., 1999; Bershtein et al., 2013; Sullivan et al., 2012; Wells, 1990; Serrano et al., 1993; and Zhang et al., 1995.

claim: Residues contributing to protein stability typically interact in an additive fashion.
source: Strikingly, however, it is relatively easy to obtain more stable proteins by mutagenesis (Matsuura et al., 1999; Bershtein et al., 2013; Sullivan et al., 2012), with the contributing residues typically interacting in an additive fashion (Wells, 1990; Serrano et al., 1993; Zhang et al., 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Wells, 1990; Serrano et al., 1993; and Zhang et al., 1995.

claim: Many examples exist in which increased stability has been achieved in laboratory modifications of proteins with few if any consequences for enzyme efficiency.
source: Many examples exist in which increased stability has been achieved in laboratory modifications of proteins with few if any consequences for enzyme efficiency (e.g. Giver et al., 1998; Zhang et al., 1995; Taverna and Goldstein, 2002; Borgo and Havranek, 2012; Moon et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Giver et al., 1998; Zhang et al., 1995; Taverna and Goldstein, 2002; Borgo and Havranek, 2012; and Moon et al., 2014.

claim: A hyperbolic relationship between fitness and the binding energy involving protein stability follows from biophysical principles.
source: A hyperbolic relationship between fitness and the binding energy involving protein stability follows from biophysical principles (Govindarajan and Goldstein, 1997; Taverna and Goldstein, 2002; Bloom et al., 2005; Zeldovich and Shakhnovich, 2008; Wylie and Shakhnovich, 2011; Serohijos and Shakhnovich, 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Govindarajan and Goldstein, 1997; Taverna and Goldstein, 2002; Bloom et al., 2005; Zeldovich and Shakhnovich, 2008; Wylie and Shakhnovich, 2011; and Serohijos and Shakhnovich, 2014.

claim: Proteins of equivalent length fold at least ten times more rapidly in bacteria than in eukaryotes.
source: Notably, proteins of equivalent length fold at least ten times more rapidly in bacteria than in eukaryotes (Galzitskaya et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Galzitskaya et al., 2011.

claim: An in vitro evaluation of the folding stability of the dihydrofolate reductase enzyme from 36 species of mesophilic bacteria shows a substantial range of variation among species, with the standard deviation being roughly 10% of the mean.
source: Moreover, an in vitro evaluation of the folding stability of the dihydrofolate reductase enzyme from 36 species of mesophilic bacteria illustrates the existence of a substantial range of variation among species, with the standard deviation being roughly 10% of the mean (Bershtein et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Bershtein et al., 2015.

claim: Similar behavior of stationary distributions was previously pointed out for the stationary distribution of allele frequencies.
source: Similar behavior was previously pointed out for the stationary distribution of allele frequencies (Wright, 1969).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Wright, 1969.

claim: Mean phenotypes are unlikely to commonly achieve states that endow a population with maximum fitness.
source: Although such traits may sometimes be under selection for an intermediate optimum, selection may often operate in a continuous directional fashion. In either case, there are two reasons why mean phenotypes are unlikely to commonly achieve states that endow a population with maximum fitness.
evidence: This is a theoretical conclusion derived from the models presented in the manuscript.

claim: If mutation bias conflicts with the directional effects of selection, the optimum phenotype will not coincide with the mean phenotype.
source: First, if mutation bias conflicts with the directional effects of selection, the optimum phenotype will not coincide with the mean phenotype.
evidence: This is a theoretical conclusion derived from the models presented in the manuscript.

claim: A drift barrier exists beyond which the gradient of the selection function is not steep enough to overcome the vagaries of genetic drift, thereby preventing further adaptive progress.
source: Second, even in the absence of mutation bias and regardless of the form of the fitness function, a drift barrier exists beyond which the gradient of the selection function is not steep enough to overcome the vagaries of genetic drift, thereby preventing further adaptive progress.
evidence: This is a theoretical conclusion derived from the models presented in the manuscript.

claim: Species with substantially different population-genetic environments may commonly exhibit measurable differences in trait means despite experiencing identical forms of directional selection.
source: These sorts of observations raise the significant possibility that species with substantially different population-genetic environments may commonly exhibit measurable differences in trait means despite experiencing identical forms of directional selection, again raising challenging issues for those who wish to interpret phenotypic differences as reflections of different underlying processes of selection.
evidence: This is a theoretical conclusion derived from the models and observations presented in the manuscript.

claim: Multimodal stationary distributions have been predicted to arise in some situations involving transcription.
source: Although the frequency of stationary distributions with multimodal forms is unknown, they have been predicted to arise in some situations involving transcription (Lynch and Hagner, 2015; Tuğrul et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Lynch and Hagner, 2015 and Tuğrul et al., 2015.

claim: The population mean phenotype wanders within a certain range over evolutionary time due to mutation, selection, and drift.
source: Owing to this latter factor, even if the forces of selection and mutation remain constant, the population mean phenotype of a trait will wander within a certain range over evolutionary time, with the frequency of occurrence of alternative mean phenotypes depending on patterns and strengths of selective and mutational effects (Figure 1).
evidence: This is illustrated in Figure 1 and explained theoretically in the text.

claim: The stationary distribution of mean phenotypes can be viewed as a summary distribution of phenotypic means across a large number of replicate populations exposed to identical conditions for a very long period.
source: The focus of this study, the stationary distribution of mean phenotypes, can be viewed as a summary distribution of: (1) phenotypic means across a large number of replicate populations exposed to identical conditions for a very long period; or (2) a historical survey of mean phenotypes in a single population over a long time period, again under constant environmental and population-genetic conditions.
evidence: This is a definition of the stationary distribution concept used in the manuscript.

claim: The stationary distribution of mean phenotypes can be viewed as a historical survey of mean phenotypes in a single population over a long time period under constant environmental and population-genetic conditions.
source: The focus of this study, the stationary distribution of mean phenotypes, can be viewed as a summary distribution of: (1) phenotypic means across a large number of replicate populations exposed to identical conditions for a very long period; or (2) a historical survey of mean phenotypes in a single population over a long time period, again under constant environmental and population-genetic conditions.
evidence: This is a definition of the stationary distribution concept used in the manuscript.

claim: Under most reasonable biological conditions, independent of the starting conditions, a stationary distribution of mean phenotypes is eventually converged upon.
source: Under most reasonable biological conditions, independent of the starting conditions, a stationary distribution of mean phenotypes (among hypothetical replicate populations) is eventually converged upon, at which point there is an exact balance between opposing forces.
evidence: This is a theoretical property of the diffusion process model used in the manuscript.

claim: With a flat mutation function, the distribution will follow that expected under selection alone.
source: Conversely, with a flat mutation function, an unlikely scenario, the distribution will follow that expected under selection alone.
evidence: This is a logical inference from Equation (1b) in the limiting case of no mutation bias.

claim: The composite parameter 4Neμ generally ranges from 0.001 to 0.1, with the lower and higher ends of the range being typical in vertebrates and microbes, respectively.
source: This composite parameter is equivalent to the amount of standing heterozygosity at neutral nucleotide sites in natural populations under mutation-drift equilibrium, and generally ranges from 0.001 to 0.1, with the lower and higher ends of the range being typical in vertebrates and microbes, respectively (Lynch, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Lynch, 2007.

claim: Under the Gaussian fitness function, the stationary distribution of mean phenotypes is Gaussian.
source: With both the selection and mutation terms in Equation (11) being Gaussian functions, the product is also Gaussian (Lande, 1976), in this case leading to a stationary distribution of mean phenotypes
evidence: This is derived mathematically and supported by citation to Lande, 1976.

claim: The hyperbolic fitness function generates a slightly asymmetric distribution of means with tail to the right.
source: Although the hyperbolic fitness function generates a slightly asymmetric distribution of means (with tail to the right), the bulk of the distribution is approximately normal
evidence: This is a mathematical property of the hyperbolic fitness function model.

claim: The bulk of the distribution under the hyperbolic fitness function is approximately normal.
source: Although the hyperbolic fitness function generates a slightly asymmetric distribution of means (with tail to the right), the bulk of the distribution is approximately normal
evidence: This is a mathematical property of the hyperbolic fitness function model.

claim: The sigmoid fitness function is sometimes called a mesa function.
source: With a sigmoid fitness function, sometimes called a mesa function (Gerland and Hwa, 2002; Berg et al., 2004), there is an inflection point such that the fitness landscape becomes progressively flatter at both higher and lower values.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Gerland and Hwa, 2002 and Berg et al., 2004.

claim: With the sigmoid fitness function, adjacent variants become increasingly similar in fitness at both extremes of the phenotype distribution.
source: This means that adjacent variants become increasingly similar in fitness (i.e. more neutral with respect to each other) at both extremes of the phenotype distribution.
evidence: This is a logical consequence of the sigmoid fitness function form.

claim: With mutation bias encouraging the mean phenotype to deviate from the optimum, the result will be a population under persistent directional selection despite the existence of an attainable but not sustainable phenotype with maximum fitness.
source: For example, with mutation bias encouraging the mean phenotype to deviate from the optimum, the result will be a population under persistent directional selection despite the existence of an attainable (but not sustainable) phenotype with maximum fitness.
evidence: This is a theoretical conclusion derived from the models presented in the manuscript.

claim: The drift barrier will ensure variation in mean phenotypes among populations exposed to identical selection pressures.
source: Even without mutation pressure and in the face of intrinsic directional selection, for example, a hyperbolic or mesa fitness function, the most common mean phenotype will not be equivalent to the optimum phenotype, and the drift barrier will ensure variation in mean phenotypes among populations exposed to identical selection pressures.
evidence: This is a theoretical conclusion derived from the models presented in the manuscript.

claim: The mean phenotypes of cellular attributes are modulated by the power of random genetic drift.
source: Although the data are not extensive, several lines of evidence support the idea that the mean phenotypes of cellular attributes are indeed modulated by the power of random genetic drift.
evidence: This is supported by the examples discussed in the manuscript, including mutation rates, enzyme efficiency, and protein stability.

claim: The scaling of mutation rate with Ne is qualitatively consistent with the drift-barrier hypothesis for mutation-rate evolution.
source: Such a scaling is qualitatively consistent with the drift-barrier hypothesis for mutation-rate evolution (Lynch, 2010; Lynch, 2011), which postulates that because most mutations are deleterious, selection will typically operate to improve replication fidelity, with refinements in molecular performance eventually being thwarted by random genetic drift
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Lynch, 2010 and Lynch, 2011.

claim: As the mutation rate is progressively lowered, there is less room for improvement and hence a narrower range of selectively advantageous replication-fidelity variants accessible by selection.
source: as the mutation rate is progressively lowered, there is less room for improvement and hence a narrower range of selectively advantageous replication-fidelity variants accessible by selection.
evidence: This is part of the drift-barrier hypothesis explanation.

claim: The fact that bacteria utilize transcription-factor binding-site motifs with stronger affinity than eukaryotes is plausibly related to a higher efficiency of selection in bacteria.
source: The fact that bacteria utilize transcription-factor binding-site motifs with stronger affinity to their cognate transcription factors than is the case in eukaryotes is also plausibly related to a higher efficiency of selection in the former (Lynch and Hagner, 2015).
evidence: This is an inference connecting the observation to the theory, supported by citation to Lynch and Hagner, 2015.

claim: It is commonly argued that marginal stability is required for proper protein function, with excess stability somehow reducing protein performance.
source: Moreover, although it is commonly argued that marginal stability is required for proper protein function, with excess stability somehow reducing protein performance, this has not held up to close scrutiny.
evidence: This is a statement about a common argument in the field that the author disputes.

claim: The argument that marginal stability is required for proper protein function has not held up to close scrutiny.
source: Moreover, although it is commonly argued that marginal stability is required for proper protein function, with excess stability somehow reducing protein performance, this has not held up to close scrutiny.
evidence: This is supported by the examples cited in the following sentence.

claim: A hyperbolic relationship between fitness and the binding energy involving protein stability follows from biophysical principles.
source: A hyperbolic relationship between fitness and the binding energy involving protein stability follows from biophysical principles (Govindarajan and Goldstein, 1997; Taverna and Goldstein, 2002; Bloom et al., 2005; Zeldovich and Shakhnovich, 2008; Wylie and Shakhnovich, 2011; Serohijos and Shakhnovich, 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Under the hyperbolic model for protein stability, proteins are expected to be pushed by natural selection to more stable configurations until reaching the point where any further fitness improvement is small enough to be offset by the vagaries of random genetic drift and/or mutation pressure towards less stable states.
source: under this model, proteins are expected to be pushed by natural selection to more stable configurations until reaching the point where any further fitness improvement is small enough to be offset by the vagaries of random genetic drift and/or mutation pressure towards less stable states.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction based on the hyperbolic fitness model and drift-barrier concept.

claim: The standard deviation of folding stability of dihydrofolate reductase enzyme from 36 species of mesophilic bacteria is roughly 10% of the mean.
source: Moreover, an in vitro evaluation of the folding stability of the dihydrofolate reductase enzyme from 36 species of mesophilic bacteria illustrates the existence of a substantial range of variation among species, with the standard deviation being roughly 10% of the mean (Bershtein et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Bershtein et al., 2015.

claim: The distribution of folding stability among bacterial species may reflect the dispersion in mean phenotypes associated with drift around the drift barrier.
source: In principle, such a distribution may reflect the dispersion in mean phenotypes associated with drift around the drift barrier.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the observed variation.

claim: The mutation function employed in this study likely comes closer to approximating the situation for cellular features than do previous functions relied on in quantitative genetics.
source: Although the mutation function employed here likely comes closer to approximating the situation for cellular features than do previous functions relied on in quantitative genetics, in reality we do not know the exact form of this function for any cellular feature.
evidence: This is the author's assessment of the mutation model used.

claim: We do not know the exact form of the mutation function for any cellular feature.
source: Although the mutation function employed here likely comes closer to approximating the situation for cellular features than do previous functions relied on in quantitative genetics, in reality we do not know the exact form of this function for any cellular feature.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge.

claim: Plausible cases exist in which the stationary distribution exhibits two peaks, one largely driven by selection and the other by mutation pressure.
source: Although the stationary distribution was unimodal in all of the cases examined above, plausible cases exist in which the stationary distribution exhibits two peaks, one largely driven by selection and the other by mutation pressure.
evidence: This is a theoretical possibility discussed in the manuscript.

claim: For a bimodal stationary distribution to occur, the gradient of mutation pressure in one direction has to be of a form such that its product with the selection gradient has an internal minimum.
source: For this to occur, the gradient of mutation pressure in one direction has to be of a form such that its product with the selection gradient has an internal minimum (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a theoretical condition for bimodality, illustrated in Figure 4.

claim: In a bimodal system, the population mean phenotype is expected to reside in two alternative semi-stable domains for extended periods of time.
source: Under such a scenario, the population mean phenotype is expected to reside in two alternative semi-stable domains for extended periods of time, with the rates of transitions between domains depending on the relative heights of the two peaks, the depth of the distributional valley, and the curvatures of the stationary distribution at the inflection points (Lande, 1985; Barton and Rouhani, 1987).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Lande, 1985 and Barton and Rouhani, 1987.

claim: Over long evolutionary time periods, a bimodal system will exhibit detailed balance with net fluxes equal in both directions.
source: Over long evolutionary time periods, such a system will exhibit detailed balance – the net fluxes will be equal in both directions, with the ratio of the occupancy of the two alternative domains being inversely related to the ratio of the transition rates between them, that is, with the less frequent domain having a higher conditional rate of transition to the more frequent domain.
evidence: This is a theoretical property of bimodal systems at equilibrium.

claim: The frequency of stationary distributions with multimodal forms is unknown.
source: Although the frequency of stationary distributions with multimodal forms is unknown, they have been predicted to arise in some situations involving transcription (Lynch and Hagner, 2015; Tuğrul et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge.

claim: Bimodal distributions may help explain the substantial and seemingly disorganized diversity of certain cellular features across the Tree of Life.
source: Such ideas may be helpful in attempts to decipher the substantial and seemingly disorganized diversity of certain cellular features such as open vs. closed mitosis (Sazer et al., 2014), the structure of the centrosome (Carvalho-Santos et al., 2011), and the variable multimeric states of proteins (Dayhoff et al., 2010; Lynch, 2013; Ahnert et al., 2015) across the Tree of Life.
evidence: This is a speculative application of the bimodal distribution theory, supported by citations to examples.
